title: Big Five Personality Traits and Financial Literacy: Effect on Risk Tolerance of Filipino Investors from Higher Education Institutions in Metro Manila
authors: Mendoza, D. M.; Padernal, A. M. G.; Pante, E. M. S.; Magbata, E. V. S.; Mandigma, M. B. S.
venue: Review of Integrative Business and Economics Research
tldr: Extraversion, openness, neuroticism, and financial literacy positively influence risk tolerance among Filipino investors from Metro Manila universities, while agreeableness and conscientiousness do not.
problem_and_motivation: Risk tolerance is a critical factor in investment decisions, but its determinants in the Philippine context remain underexplored. Prior studies show inconsistent findings on the role of personality and financial literacy. This study addresses the gap by testing their influence on Filipino investors.
approach: Surveyed 320 students and faculty from Metro Manila higher education institutions with at least PHP 1,000 invested in stocks, bonds, or cryptocurrency.
Used adapted and modified questionnaires for Big Five Personality Traits (23 items), financial literacy (20 items), and risk tolerance (11 items).
Employed a 4-point Likert scale and established reliability via Cronbach's Alpha (0.881–0.918).
Applied multiple regression analysis to test the influence of personality traits and financial literacy on risk tolerance.
Included age and monthly family income as control variables in a secondary regression model.
findings: num: 43.6% of the variation in risk tolerance is explained by personality traits and financial literacy (R² = 0.436).
num: 45.1% of variation is explained when age and income are added as controls (R² = 0.451).
Extraversion, openness, and neuroticism significantly and positively influence risk tolerance (p < 0.05).
Financial literacy has the strongest positive influence on risk tolerance (β = 0.504, p = 0.000).
Agreeableness and conscientiousness do not significantly influence risk tolerance.
Monthly family income negatively influences risk tolerance when included as a control variable.
Age was not a significant predictor of risk tolerance.
key_figures_tables: Figure 1: Hypothesized model showing personality traits and financial literacy as independent variables → Predicts risk tolerance as dependent variable.
Table 1: Cronbach's Alpha values for Big Five (0.913), financial literacy (0.918), risk tolerance (0.881) → All constructs show high internal consistency.
Table 2: Demographic profile of 320 respondents → 92.81% aged 18-25, 68.75% female, 89.06% students.
Table 3: Descriptive statistics with means and standard deviations → Openness has highest mean (3.18), neuroticism lowest (2.67).
Table 4: Multiple regression results without controls → Extraversion, openness, neuroticism, and financial literacy are significant.
Table 5: Multiple regression with age and income controls → Financial literacy (β=0.513) and neuroticism (β=0.140) remain significant.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper contributes empirical evidence on the determinants of risk tolerance in the Philippine context, which has been underexplored. It validates the predictive utility of the Big Five Personality Model for financial behavior in a non-Western setting. The study also reinforces the role of financial literacy as a key driver of investment risk tolerance. It highlights which personality traits are relevant and which are not, offering direction for future research. The findings add to the behavioral finance literature by confirming cross-cultural applicability of some established relationships.

topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: A systematic scan across all topic domains was performed. Domains 1.A and 1.C were flagged as high relevance because the paper directly studies Filipino young adults' financial behavior. Domain 3.A was marked contextual because financial literacy includes management ability but not explicit categorization. Domains 5.A and 5.C were flagged high and low respectively: 5.A fits directly as the paper examines personality-based behavioral profiles, while 5.C is low because it uses regression rather than classification. Domain 6.A was considered low because the predictive aspect is ancillary. Domain 7.A was contextual due to the budgeting implication of financial literacy. Domains 10.A and 10.B were contextual due to privacy mention. Domain 12.A was low because evaluation focuses on statistical model fit, not a system. Other domains (2.A, 2.B, 2.C, 2.D, 3.B, 3.C, 4.A, 4.B, 5.B, 6.B, 7.B, 7.C, 7.D, 7.E, 8.A, 8.B, 8.C, 9.A, 9.B, 9.C, 10.C, 11.A, 11.B, 12.C, 13.A, 13.B, 13.C, 14.A, 14.B, 14.C) were rejected as they were not addressed by the paper. The overall topical coverage centers on behavioral finance and investor psychology.
